title: Renew our days (Lamentations 5:21)
hook: the book's closing plea, "renew our days as of old", sung as the Torah returns to the ark

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the middle of Lamentations, mercies new every morning. Your line was new every morning. What new thing did you find? Today, the last lines of the book, and a custom that won't let it end where it ends. Day eight hundred sixty-three.

Some books end on a wedding, some on a homecoming. Lamentations ends on a verse that is hard to say out loud in a room full of mourners. The line just before it has had a longer life. Two weeks ago, this path heard the tree-of-life verses sung as the Torah scroll goes back into the ark. Right after them, as the doors close, comes this line, lifted from the last page of a book of ruins. Today's word is that line.
screen: `A HARD LAST VERSE.` → `THE LINE JUST BEFORE IT.` → `SUNG AS THE ARK CLOSES.`

segments.voice: Renew our days. The verse in full, in the JPS 1917 translation: "Turn Thou us unto Thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; Renew our days as of old." In Hebrew it begins hashivenu: turn us, bring us back. It asks for two things. First, turn us. Not, we will turn ourselves; turn us, and we will be turned. Then, renew our days as of old, kekedem, as before. Not a brand-new life. The old days, made new again. Now the hard part. That isn't the book's last verse. The last verse, in the same translation, reads: "Thou canst not have utterly rejected us, And be exceeding wroth against us!" The Hebrew is hard to pin down. Those translators heard a protest: surely you haven't cast us off for good. Other readers hear a plain statement that God has rejected them, or a fearful question left hanging. Either way, the book doesn't tie a bow. Jewish custom does something tender with that. When Lamentations is read aloud in public, the reader doesn't stop on the last verse. After it, the plea before it is said again: turn us, renew our days. So the congregation never closes the book on that cry. They close it on a request. The custom doesn't change a word of the text. It changes where the voice comes to rest. Even the JPS 1917 printing sets the plea again, in brackets, after the last verse. And the plea travels. When the Torah returns to the ark, the congregation sings hashivenu as the doors close. A line from a city in ruins becomes the line sung over a scroll going home. Renew our days: a plea that has already been through the worst, and still asks.
screen: `TURN US, AND WE SHALL BE TURNED.` · `THE OLD DAYS, MADE NEW.` · then, large: `THE LAST VERSE: CAST OFF FOR GOOD?` · then: `READERS REPEAT THE PLEA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for renewal. Think of one part of your life that has gone dry: a friendship, a habit you used to love, a way of paying attention that faded. Don't try to invent something new. Remember how it was when it was alive. Then ask, in whatever way you ask for things, for it to be renewed. If you pray, you can use the verse itself: renew our days as of old. The bell holds the time.
Renew our days. The plea near the end of Lamentations: turn us back, and make our days new, as of old. Today's word.
Your line: renew our days. Today, pick up one old good thing you'd let slip, and do it once more. Day eight hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: When Lamentations is read aloud on Tisha B'Av, the next-to-last verse is repeated after the final one, and 'hashivenu' is sung in synagogue as the Torah scroll is returned to the ark.
